distribution-idea.t: A distribution says **which values a random variable can take and how likely each one is**. The taller the bar, the more likely the value. Named distributions are ready-made shapes for common situations.

bernoulli.t: A Bernoulli variable is **0 or 1**. With **p = 0.3**, “spam” (1) has probability **0.3** and “not spam” (0) has **0.7**. Every binary label in classification is a Bernoulli outcome.

binomial.t: Count the spam emails among **10**, each spam with probability 0.3. The count is **Binomial**. Three is the most likely (about **0.27**); zero is rare (about **0.03**).

uniform.t: A Uniform variable on **[0, 1]** treats every part of the range alike: equal-width slices are **equally likely**. It models “no preference”.

gaussian.t: The Gaussian is a symmetric bell around its mean **μ**. Its width is the standard deviation **σ**, and about **68%** of the values fall within one σ of the mean. It fits quantities built from many small effects, like measurement noise.

compare.t: **Bernoulli and Binomial** are for counts of yes/no events. **Uniform and Gaussian** are for continuous values. The shape of each tells what kind of data it describes.

choose-model.t: Start from the question. A yes/no label: **Bernoulli**. How many yeses in n tries: **Binomial**. No preference over a range: **Uniform**. A continuous value clustered around a typical one: **Gaussian**.

ml-connection.t: Models quietly assume distributions. **Classification treats a label as Bernoulli; linear regression treats the noise as Gaussian.** Choosing the right one is choosing the right model of the data.
